content:Speaker user says: How can you make sure your sound system is set up to deliver the best sound experience at a Super Bowl party?: Chances are you, your significant other, your parents, and at least half of your friends are looking for somewhere to watch the big game this Sunday. Before you look into which pubs have the biggest televisions, why not host your own party? You really don’t need to be a huge football buff throw a wicked party that people will enjoy just as much as the game. Here are few tips to make sure your party is as entertaining and crowd pleasing as the game itself.
Invite your guests in advance – Sounds like common sense but like I said, everyone is looking for somewhere to watch the game. So make sure you invite your guests in advance to ensure a good turnout and to make sure you can plan accordingly.
Food, food, and more food – Perhaps the most important part of a football party, besides the actual game. The Super Bowl is one of the biggest events for food consumption and trust me, your guests will expect to indulge regardless of where the party is held. Stick with some classics that you can prepare ahead of time, like chili and pulled pork, but also provide a mixture of finger foods that guests can munch on throughout the entire game. Check out our SUNSET® favorites for football inspired appetizers.
Pump up the volume – This is going to be a loud party, whether you want it to be or not. Make sure your sound system is set up to deliver the best sound experience you can. This will ensure that no play goes missed and will get your party in the spirit. If you really want your guests to feel like they’re at the game, give them some fun sound makers like thundersticks and cowbells (of course, at your discretion).
Place your bets– Part of the fun of watching the Super Bowl is placing bets on the game. Having guests bet on a variety of things like the final score, number of fumbles, length of the halftime show, etc. Will get your guests into the game and make it a far more interactive experience. Plus, if someone gets to leave the party with a prize AND bragging rights, you can bet they’ll be attending your party again next year.
Support the teams – Make sure you know what teams are competing so you can prepare your décor accordingly. Even something as simple as having plates and cups in the color-scheme of the two teams will amp up the atmosphere. The more themed décor you have, the better in my books.
By following these easy guidelines, your football party is sure to get everyone cheering – even the ones that are there for the commercials. content:Speaker user says: Generate response to the question/instruction based on a piece of given material

Question/Instruction: What do architects mean by seeking a "wholeness" in their designs, and how is this different from the approach taken by architects in the past?

Given material: THE VERY IDEA OF a face lift goes against the grain of most architects' thinking. Their instincts lean much more toward all-out plastic surgery, reshaping the body to take on a whole different cast. That is, if they are willing to keep the old body at all. Throwing it out and starting from scratch probably gets closer to their way of doing things.
Architects, so the common wisdom goes, want to remake the world, or at least as much of it as they can get their hands on. It's been true enough in the past, but has become less and less so in the last decade, as the architectural profession has been forced to face twin realities: the growing preference in our society both for preserving older buildings and for renovating what we have, rather than starting over again. Renovation is usually, though not always, cheaper than new construction, which makes it especially appealing in an age of monetary constraints. So it is partly a matter of esthetics, partly economics and partly common sense that have brought us here. But we are clearly at a moment when few architects dare to treat a renovation project as if it were a blank slate.
A generation ago, architects were taught that their mission was to leave a mark, and often, the stronger the better. New buildings were designed to stand out from their surroundings; renovations of older ones were done so that no one could fail to see the difference between the original and the addition. Even architects whose careers began relatively recently tended to operate this way. Think, for example, of Michael Graves, the Princeton, N.J.-based architect who in the late 1960's and early 70's first came into public view through the striking modernist additions he put onto older houses (which led some colleagues to dub him the ''Cubist kitchen king''). The very point of Graves's additions was to stand apart from the houses to which they were attached. They were highly abstract objects, possessed of far more sophistication than the original houses, and their aloofness was part of the architectural message. ''You are common, but I am something much more special,'' the additions seemed to sneer at the houses.
The attitude of Graves's early years was hardly his alone. At the beginning of the 70's, the New York City firm of Mayers & Schiff designed an addition to an old clapboard farmhouse in Connecticut in the form of a two-story-high cedar and glass box. Lest there be any mistake about the transition from new to old, the box was set at a diagonal from the original house and wrapped around one of its corners, the new literally encasing the old.
Even Robert A. M. Stern, an architect whose career has soared in the last decade, largely due to his success in reproducing traditional architectural styles, nonetheless felt that he could not afford to let his own work disappear beside that of another architect. At least that is what one major addition he completed in 1981 would suggest. The house is a huge Georgian-style mansion in Llewelyn Park, N.J.; the addition, which contains an indoor pool, is best described as something of an English Baroque pleasure pavilion with a greenhouse roof. And while it picks up a few details from the original house, no one could say it blends in softly.
IT IS TEMPTING TO think of the whole issue in terms of ego, given how much, even today, our image of the architect is shaped by such fictitious characters as Howard Roark in the Ayn Rand novel ''The Fountainhead.'' Her architect-hero stands defiantly against bourgeois taste, and would sooner burn his T-square than design a building that took its cues from anyone else's. But for all we might want to see the architect as a romantic hero - for all architects might want to see themselves as such - the truth is that most architecture is shaped by the prevailing taste of an age.
As a matter of fact, ego has relatively little to do with it. Indeed, in recent years some of the biggest egos in architecture have begun to do some of the most restrained work. Kevin Roche, who gave us the monumental additions to The Metropolitan Museum of Art in the 70's - wings whose glass and limestone forms contrast sharply with the classical, older sections of the Met - recently designed an addition to the Jewish Museum on Fifth Avenue that is simply an exact reproduction of the museum's original French Gothic mansion. The addition, which will go into construction later this year, is conceived as if to blend new and old into a seamless whole.
Similarly, Romaldo Giurgola, a winner of the American Institute of Architects' highest award, has proposed adding to Louis I. Kahn's Kimbell Museum of Art in Fort Worth by literally extending its design at each end. That project hasn't been received as well as the Roche plan, largely because the Kimbell, unlike the Jewish Museum, is considered to be one of the great works of American architecture. Tampering with it at all, even by replicating the original, has been viewed by many critics as akin to adding a few strokes to a Caravaggio.
These two examples are extreme ones, of course. Precisely duplicating what has come before is hardly the only mode of the hour, particularly for public buildings. But it is being done more and more. And the fact that architects of Giurgola's stature, or Roche's, would consider replicating sections of older buildings tells us how much architectural values have changed.
In the last few years, there has been less hubris in architectural design, less of the arrogant certainty that we can do much better than the architects of earlier generations, and much less of the patronizing attitude toward tradition that for many architects was the motivation for breaking away from the old style when designing a renovation or addition. The original building was there first - a simple fact, but one that today has come to earn it a certain degree of respect. We do not condescend to Georgian or Tudor or Shingle Style houses the way we once did. And we are much more likely now to understand how good the average, traditionally styled American house built before 1940 really is. Architects today know better than to treat it with scorn.
MORE THAN INSISTENT originality, we seek a kind of wholeness now, a sense that a building is part of a larger continuity. And if that means the architect is going to be able to express his or her own design sensibility slightly less, we seem to feel that it is a fair trade-off. By the same token, an expanded or renovated house need not look merely like a bigger version of what was there before. But it should take its cues from the original building. Sometimes those cues can be interpreted literally; in other circumstances, it makes more sense to let the original building set a tone, a direction to which the second architect can respond. If architecture can be thought of as a conversation, the new architect entering the house doesn't need to repeat the words of the first architect - but he or she at least ought to be speaking the same language.
A couple of recent examples: In Larchmont, N.Y., in 1987, the architects Karen Bausman and Leslie Gill of Bausman-Gill Associates completed a two-story modernist addition to a tiny one-story stucco cottage. To have the extra space they wanted yet still preserve several valued trees on the small plot, the addition had to be two stories tall. Had it imitated the Arts and Crafts style of the cottage, it would have risked overwhelming the original building. But the finished addition appears neither to dominate the cottage nor to be incompatible with it. Bausman-Gill used the same material, stucco, as in the original building and similar steel casement windows, allowing the cottage to initiate the conversation, so to speak. The result is a deft marriage of old and new, the whole being both comfortable and visually richer than either section could be on its own.
Similarly, the San Francisco architect Mark Mack took a less literal direction in his addition to a rough-concrete modern house of the 60's, set high in the hills of Berkeley, Calif. Mack's own work has a blunt, almost primitive quality to it, which created a certain compatibility at the outset. But the addition, completed in 1988, stands out sharply from the original building: Its stucco walls are painted a rusty red with indigo-blue trim, and it reads as a powerful sculptural presence on its own. Still, it was not built to stand alone, and doesn't. The addition and the original house strengthen each other, forming a complex and vivid whole. (Mack considered a scheme that was more literally derived from the original house, and left it up to the clients to decide how assertive they wanted him to be. He was pleased with their decision; the other scheme, he felt, was too accommodating.) While the version that was built is hardly indifferent to the original building, it strikes out independently - yet in a way that relates continually to the original, engaging it in a vibrant architectural dialogue.
The conversation is quieter on Long Island, where David Hannaford Mitchell transformed a huge white clapboard farmhouse in Remsenburg into a rambling but vastly more genteel house. The changes Mitchell made are quite dramatic. He took a bland building and refined it, adding shutters, multipaned windows, a cornice and decks framed in subtly detailed latticework. Inside, the rooms were reorganized to flow gracefully into one another. The result, which was finished in 1987, is a lively and energetic composition that manages not to be overrefined or precious. The basic strength of the big old farmhouse is still there: It has been dressed up on the outside and opened up inside to just the right degree to bring out its architectural potential.
And so it is with all of the best renovations. They do not defy or sneer at the buildings to which they are appended, but support them. Sometimes buildings are supported best simply by being continued or extended, sometimes by being altered quite dramatically. The point is that whatever is done, it is the original building that sets the tone. context:Architects embracing wholeness keywords: architects, wholeness, context, aesthetics, renovation, ego, architectural style, traditional, continuity, design sensibility, preservation, dialogue, renovation, landmark, landmark, expression, intervention, monumental, sculptural, restoration tags: architects, wholeness, design, continuity, design sensibility, renovation

content:Speaker user says: Here is a piece of text: THE VERY IDEA OF a face lift goes against the grain of most architects' thinking. Their instincts lean much more toward all-out plastic surgery, reshaping the body to take on a whole different cast. That is, if they are willing to keep the old body at all. Throwing it out and starting from scratch probably gets closer to their way of doing things.
Architects, so the common wisdom goes, want to remake the world, or at least as much of it as they can get their hands on. It's been true enough in the past, but has become less and less so in the last decade, as the architectural profession has been forced to face twin realities: the growing preference in our society both for preserving older buildings and for renovating what we have, rather than starting over again. Renovation is usually, though not always, cheaper than new construction, which makes it especially appealing in an age of monetary constraints. So it is partly a matter of esthetics, partly economics and partly common sense that have brought us here. But we are clearly at a moment when few architects dare to treat a renovation project as if it were a blank slate.
A generation ago, architects were taught that their mission was to leave a mark, and often, the stronger the better. New buildings were designed to stand out from their surroundings; renovations of older ones were done so that no one could fail to see the difference between the original and the addition. Even architects whose careers began relatively recently tended to operate this way. Think, for example, of Michael Graves, the Princeton, N.J.-based architect who in the late 1960's and early 70's first came into public view through the striking modernist additions he put onto older houses (which led some colleagues to dub him the ''Cubist kitchen king''). The very point of Graves's additions was to stand apart from the houses to which they were attached. They were highly abstract objects, possessed of far more sophistication than the original houses, and their aloofness was part of the architectural message. ''You are common, but I am something much more special,'' the additions seemed to sneer at the houses.
The attitude of Graves's early years was hardly his alone. At the beginning of the 70's, the New York City firm of Mayers & Schiff designed an addition to an old clapboard farmhouse in Connecticut in the form of a two-story-high cedar and glass box. Lest there be any mistake about the transition from new to old, the box was set at a diagonal from the original house and wrapped around one of its corners, the new literally encasing the old.
Even Robert A. M. Stern, an architect whose career has soared in the last decade, largely due to his success in reproducing traditional architectural styles, nonetheless felt that he could not afford to let his own work disappear beside that of another architect. At least that is what one major addition he completed in 1981 would suggest. The house is a huge Georgian-style mansion in Llewelyn Park, N.J.; the addition, which contains an indoor pool, is best described as something of an English Baroque pleasure pavilion with a greenhouse roof. And while it picks up a few details from the original house, no one could say it blends in softly.
IT IS TEMPTING TO think of the whole issue in terms of ego, given how much, even today, our image of the architect is shaped by such fictitious characters as Howard Roark in the Ayn Rand novel ''The Fountainhead.'' Her architect-hero stands defiantly against bourgeois taste, and would sooner burn his T-square than design a building that took its cues from anyone else's. But for all we might want to see the architect as a romantic hero - for all architects might want to see themselves as such - the truth is that most architecture is shaped by the prevailing taste of an age.
As a matter of fact, ego has relatively little to do with it. Indeed, in recent years some of the biggest egos in architecture have begun to do some of the most restrained work. Kevin Roche, who gave us the monumental additions to The Metropolitan Museum of Art in the 70's - wings whose glass and limestone forms contrast sharply with the classical, older sections of the Met - recently designed an addition to the Jewish Museum on Fifth Avenue that is simply an exact reproduction of the museum's original French Gothic mansion. The addition, which will go into construction later this year, is conceived as if to blend new and old into a seamless whole.
Similarly, Romaldo Giurgola, a winner of the American Institute of Architects' highest award, has proposed adding to Louis I. Kahn's Kimbell Museum of Art in Fort Worth by literally extending its design at each end. That project hasn't been received as well as the Roche plan, largely because the Kimbell, unlike the Jewish Museum, is considered to be one of the great works of American architecture. Tampering with it at all, even by replicating the original, has been viewed by many critics as akin to adding a few strokes to a Caravaggio.
These two examples are extreme ones, of course. Precisely duplicating what has come before is hardly the only mode of the hour, particularly for public buildings. But it is being done more and more. And the fact that architects of Giurgola's stature, or Roche's, would consider replicating sections of older buildings tells us how much architectural values have changed.
In the last few years, there has been less hubris in architectural design, less of the arrogant certainty that we can do much better than the architects of earlier generations, and much less of the patronizing attitude toward tradition that for many architects was the motivation for breaking away from the old style when designing a renovation or addition. The original building was there first - a simple fact, but one that today has come to earn it a certain degree of respect. We do not condescend to Georgian or Tudor or Shingle Style houses the way we once did. And we are much more likely now to understand how good the average, traditionally styled American house built before 1940 really is. Architects today know better than to treat it with scorn.
MORE THAN INSISTENT originality, we seek a kind of wholeness now, a sense that a building is part of a larger continuity. And if that means the architect is going to be able to express his or her own design sensibility slightly less, we seem to feel that it is a fair trade-off. By the same token, an expanded or renovated house need not look merely like a bigger version of what was there before. But it should take its cues from the original building. Sometimes those cues can be interpreted literally; in other circumstances, it makes more sense to let the original building set a tone, a direction to which the second architect can respond. If architecture can be thought of as a conversation, the new architect entering the house doesn't need to repeat the words of the first architect - but he or she at least ought to be speaking the same language.
A couple of recent examples: In Larchmont, N.Y., in 1987, the architects Karen Bausman and Leslie Gill of Bausman-Gill Associates completed a two-story modernist addition to a tiny one-story stucco cottage. To have the extra space they wanted yet still preserve several valued trees on the small plot, the addition had to be two stories tall. Had it imitated the Arts and Crafts style of the cottage, it would have risked overwhelming the original building. But the finished addition appears neither to dominate the cottage nor to be incompatible with it. Bausman-Gill used the same material, stucco, as in the original building and similar steel casement windows, allowing the cottage to initiate the conversation, so to speak. The result is a deft marriage of old and new, the whole being both comfortable and visually richer than either section could be on its own.
Similarly, the San Francisco architect Mark Mack took a less literal direction in his addition to a rough-concrete modern house of the 60's, set high in the hills of Berkeley, Calif. Mack's own work has a blunt, almost primitive quality to it, which created a certain compatibility at the outset. But the addition, completed in 1988, stands out sharply from the original building: Its stucco walls are painted a rusty red with indigo-blue trim, and it reads as a powerful sculptural presence on its own. Still, it was not built to stand alone, and doesn't. The addition and the original house strengthen each other, forming a complex and vivid whole. (Mack considered a scheme that was more literally derived from the original house, and left it up to the clients to decide how assertive they wanted him to be. He was pleased with their decision; the other scheme, he felt, was too accommodating.) While the version that was built is hardly indifferent to the original building, it strikes out independently - yet in a way that relates continually to the original, engaging it in a vibrant architectural dialogue.
The conversation is quieter on Long Island, where David Hannaford Mitchell transformed a huge white clapboard farmhouse in Remsenburg into a rambling but vastly more genteel house. The changes Mitchell made are quite dramatic. He took a bland building and refined it, adding shutters, multipaned windows, a cornice and decks framed in subtly detailed latticework. Inside, the rooms were reorganized to flow gracefully into one another. The result, which was finished in 1987, is a lively and energetic composition that manages not to be overrefined or precious. The basic strength of the big old farmhouse is still there: It has been dressed up on the outside and opened up inside to just the right degree to bring out its architectural potential.
And so it is with all of the best renovations. They do not defy or sneer at the buildings to which they are appended, but support them. Sometimes buildings are supported best simply by being continued or extended, sometimes by being altered quite dramatically. The point is that whatever is done, it is the original building that sets the tone.

In ancient Egypt, furniture was often made from heavy, ornately carved woods, and featured symbolic motifs such as the lotus flower and the serpent to evoke religious beliefs related to resurrection, renewal, and immortality.

In medieval Europe, furniture design was often influenced by religious art, with elaborate carvings depicting religious stories and symbols. Gothic and Renaissance designs had a focus on the intricate carving of wood or stone, while Baroque designs embraced luxury, with rich materials like silk, velvet, and gold leaf, and flamboyant, rounded details.

During the Industrial Revolution in the 19th century, mass-produced furniture became more available, leading to a shift towards more minimalistic designs. The Arts and Crafts movement, specifically in Britain, emphasized the importance of traditional craftsmanship, simplicity, and functionality as opposed to commercialism.

In the 20th century, furniture design became more influenced by modernism, with a focus on simplicity, clean lines, and functionality. Bauhaus, a school founded in Germany in 1919, had a significant influence on modern furniture design. It emphasized the integration between art, craft and architecture, leading to a focus on utility, efficiency, and materials such as steel, glass and concrete.

Today, furniture design is influenced by both traditionalism and modernism, but new technology and materials are advancing the field. Eco-friendliness is now a significant part of furniture design, leading to the use of renewable materials such as bamboo, recycled plastics, and even repurposed wood from old buildings or furniture.

In summary, furniture design has evolved over time, and cultural norms have shaped these changes. Functionality, religion, craftsmanship, fashion, and environmental considerations all played a significant role in changing the appearance, materials, and uses of furniture. context:This text outlines the historical evolution of furniture design, highlighting how cultural norms, religious beliefs, craftsmanship, and evolving societal values have shaped the styles and materials used in furniture over time. keywords: furniture, design, cultural norms, evolution, functionality, religion, craftsmanship, materials tags: Furniture Design, History, Culture, Art, Architecture, Materials, Sustainability

content:Speaker assistant says: 1. Know your target audience: To ensure that your articles are engaging and interesting, you must first know your target audience. Understand their interests, needs, and pain points. This knowledge will enable you to write articles that appeal to them and provide relevant information.

2. Create a catchy headline: A headline is the first thing that readers see, and it can make or break your article. Therefore, create a catchy headline that intrigues readers and makes them want to read more.

3. Use an active voice: Using an active voice is not only more engaging, but it also makes your article easier to read. Write in a conversational tone to make the reader feel like they are having a conversation with you.

4. Avoid jargon: Unless you are writing for a specific audience that understands the terms, avoid using jargon. Use simple and understandable language that all readers can understand.

5. Add visuals: Images, videos, and infographics help to break up the text and make it more engaging. Use visuals to illustrate your points and make your article more appealing.

6. Tell a story: People love stories, and incorporating a narrative into your article will make it more interesting. Use anecdotes or real-life examples to bring your point home.

7. Provide value: Ensure that your article provides value to the reader. Whether it is informative or entertaining, ensure that the reader leaves with something they did not know before.

8. End with a call to action: A call to action encourages readers to engage with your content, whether it is through sharing, commenting or subscribing. End your article with a call to action that keeps readers engaged with your content. context:A professional suggests understanding the target audience is crucial for creating effective articles, ensuring content resonates and provides genuine value to readers. keywords: audience, article, engagement, content tags: writing, engagement, article, storytelling, reliable sources

3. Simplify your language: Often, it's better to err on the side of simplicity rather than trying to impress your reader with complex vocabulary or convoluted sentences. Use short, straightforward sentences and clear, simple language.

4. Use active voice: Writing in the active voice (e.g. "I wrote the essay" rather than "the essay was written by me") can make your writing more engaging and vivid.

5. Cut unnecessary words: Be ruthless in editing your work, and cut out any words or phrases that don't add anything to your writing. This will help you get to the point more quickly and make your writing more concise.

6. Use concrete details: Whenever possible, use specific details and examples to illustrate your points. This will make your writing more vivid and help your reader relate to what you're saying. context:This text offers guidance on enhancing writing skills, emphasizing regular practice, reading widely, simplifying language, using active voice, and eliminating unnecessary words to create more engaging and concise prose. keywords: writing, style, improvement, practice tags: writing, style, clarity, expression, engagement, storytelling
